title: Insufficient evidence of who granted or received live-location access
description: If the backend does not create trustworthy records of the grant decision and subsequent sharing, parties may later deny that access was granted, accepted, or used. This weakens accountability for sensitive child-location disclosures.
assumptions: Audit logging, timestamping, or receipt mechanisms may be absent or insufficient.
uncertainty_note: Repudiation relevance depends on whether accountability for grant/share events is in scope; subtree id is approximate.

title: Live-location updates are linkable over time to the same child and guardian relationship
description: Because the backend provides ongoing live-location data to the same secondary guardian account, successive updates can be linked to build a persistent profile of the child's movements and the relationship between child, primary account, and secondary guardian.
assumptions: Updates are associated with stable account or child identifiers across sessions.
uncertainty_note: Linkability is inherent to recurring live-location sharing, but exact threat-tree node id is approximate.

title: Partner can link shared analytics to app-, campaign-, or cohort-level identifiers over time
description: Even if described as aggregated, recurring analytics exports can contain stable dimensions such as app instance segment, campaign, geography, device class, or time bucket. The advertising/analytics partner may combine these with its own datasets to link multiple disclosures to the same audience segment or publisher, enabling longitudinal profiling beyond the app's original context.
assumptions: Assumes the shared analytics include persistent dimensions or sufficiently granular breakdowns across repeated transfers, rather than one-off coarse summary statistics only.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-judgement because the retrieved context gives applicable threat types by interaction but not detailed tree nodes.

title: Aggregated analytics may still identify users or very small groups
description: Usage and engagement analytics sent to the partner may include rare combinations of attributes, sparse cohorts, or small time/location buckets. These can permit singling out or inference of a specific user or tiny group, especially when the partner already has auxiliary data from advertising ecosystems.
assumptions: Assumes aggregation thresholds, k-anonymity-style controls, or suppression of small cells are absent or weak.
uncertainty_note: Applies if aggregation is not sufficiently coarse; if only heavily thresholded summaries are shared, this risk is reduced.

title: Partner can infer sensitive interests and behavior from engagement patterns
description: The destination can analyze received engagement metrics to infer user interests, routines, susceptibility to ads, or potentially sensitive app-usage patterns. Even without direct identifiers, behavioral aggregates can reveal personal or group characteristics and support audience profiling for advertising purposes.
assumptions: Assumes the app category or event taxonomy is meaningful enough that engagement statistics reveal interests or traits.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; the threat is destination-side detectability/inference from received analytics.

title: Users may be unaware that their usage data contributes to third-party advertising analytics
description: Sharing backend analytics with an advertising/analytics partner to fund a free tier can be non-obvious to users, especially when collection occurs server-side rather than directly in the mobile app. This can deprive users of awareness that their activity contributes to third-party profiling or monetization.
assumptions: Assumes privacy notices or in-product disclosures are incomplete, unclear, or bundled in a way users are unlikely to understand.
uncertainty_note: Located at the destination because the deprivation stems from the partner receiving/processing the data, though source-side disclosure shortcomings may also contribute.

title: Secondary advertising use may exceed the original service-improvement context
description: Analytics collected from app usage may originally arise from providing the service, but once shared to an advertising/analytics partner they can be reused for ad targeting, audience modeling, measurement across clients, or other secondary purposes. Such repurposing can be incompatible with users' reasonable expectations.
assumptions: Assumes contractual or technical controls do not strictly confine the partner to narrow, compatible analytics purposes.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-judgement; exact LINDDUN Pro subtree for secondary use was not provided in context.

title: Sharing analytics with an advertising partner may lack a valid legal basis or exceed consent
description: Using app-usage analytics to fund a free tier via an advertising/analytics partner may require consent or another specific legal basis, particularly where analytics support advertising, profiling, or cross-context measurement. If users were not properly informed or did not validly agree, the transfer and downstream processing may be non-compliant.
assumptions: Assumes the relevant jurisdiction treats these analytics and partner uses as requiring consent or strict purpose limitation/compliance measures.
uncertainty_note: Compliance depends heavily on jurisdiction, exact data fields, contract terms, and whether the partner acts as processor or independent controller.

title: Child can be linked across repeated SOS/check-in submissions
description: The check-in/SOS flow carries stable identifiers and precise location tied to the child, allowing the backend to link multiple submissions over time to the same child and build a movement/event history.
assumptions: Assumes the message is associated with an account, device ID, child profile, or authenticated session so repeated messages are linkable.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include specific Linkability nodes.

title: SOS/check-in message reveals the child's identity and current location
description: The flow explicitly contains highly identifying personal data: the child's message content plus current location, and likely account/session metadata. This can identify the child and reveal where they are at that moment.
assumptions: Assumes the backend can associate the message with a specific child or household account.
uncertainty_note: Specific Identifiability node id is inferred from general LINDDUN structure, not from the retrieved snippets.

title: Submitted SOS/check-in creates attributable evidence about the child
description: The backend receives a record that can serve as evidence that this child/account sent an SOS or check-in from a particular place and time. That attributable record may later be used against the child's interests if they cannot plausibly deny it.
assumptions: Assumes the backend stores message content, timestamps, account identifiers, device identifiers, or network metadata.

title: Emergency signaling and location expose sensitive behavior and circumstances
description: A manual check-in/SOS with current location may disclose very private facts, such as distress, routines, school/home presence, social relationships, or visits to sensitive places. Even the act of sending an SOS can disclose that the child is in trouble.
assumptions: Assumes location is sufficiently precise and messages are retained or observable by backend operators or downstream recipients.
uncertainty_note: Specific Detectability/Disclosure-adjacent node numbering may vary; node id is best-effort.

title: Child may not have meaningful choice or transparency over sending/storing SOS location data
description: Because the flow sends precise real-time location and emergency content about a child, the processing may exceed what the child understands or can freely consent to. Risks include insufficient notice, inadequate parental/guardian basis, unclear retention, or secondary use beyond the emergency purpose.
assumptions: Assumes the app may not provide age-appropriate notice, granular controls, or a clearly defined lawful basis and retention policy for this specific emergency flow.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance applicability depends on the actual consent/legal-basis, transparency, and retention design, which are not provided.
